"The slowdown of Starlink/Starshield and the inexplicable lack of advance warning of Russian missile launches have already caused Ukrainian civilians to die unnecessarily," wrote Branson. "How much worse can it get?" 

"If one thing is clear it’s that European leaders must overcome the initial shock about Trump’s recent actions and step up to the plate. "All options should be on the table now, from the transfer of frozen Russian assets to Ukraine to the delivery of advanced weapons systems such as Germany’s Taurus."

"Why oh why is this happening? We cannot let the free world be dismantled before our very eyes," Branson concluded.

Years after her father was gone, Jennifer Grant found herself on the floor of her Santa Monica living room, surrounded by the boxes he had left behind. 

Inside were reels of home movies, stacks of cassette tapes, childhood notes, drawings, and even a tiny tea set. One film captured a simple 1971 afternoon of the two of them skipping and laughing together. 

Hollywood had spent decades preserving Cary Grant the movie star. Her father had spent those same years quietly preserving the ordinary evidence of being her dad.

Jennifer was born in Los Angeles in February 1966, when Cary was 62. Shortly afterward he stepped away from acting for good. Walk, Don’t Run became his final feature. 

“He retired to be with me,” she later said. “That is hard to believe in and of itself. He put all of his focus, really, on me.” Fame had claimed the first half of his life. Fatherhood claimed what remained.

Her parents divorced when she was two, so her childhood moved between two households. She spent every other weekend with her father, plus Mondays and portions of school vacations; when her mother was away working, the stays grew longer. 

Cary could be exacting. She received a one-dollar weekly allowance and kept an 11:30 p.m. curfew until she was twenty. 

At Dodger Stadium they ate hot dogs even when sitting in the owner’s box. Birthday parties were arranged so that no child sat empty-handed while the guest of honor opened presents. 

He taught her to ride a bicycle and a horse. At home he recorded her baby talk, filmed bath time, and kept drawings most parents would have discarded.

She did not fully grasp the scale of what he had saved until after he died. 

The tapes became a game as she grew older. In one childhood photograph she stands on the patio at two or three, pretending to speak into the recorder. He rarely listened to the recordings himself. 

He made them for the daughter who would one day be older than the little girl whose voice he was capturing. He knew he had become a father late. 

The private man she knew—laughing in their Beverly Hills farmhouse, sharing meals, calling them both “Ollie” in a playful Cockney accent—was the version she wanted remembered. He could dine with royalty, yet one of her clearest memories from Monaco was simply playing the board game Operation with Princess Stephanie.

In his later years he asked her, more than once, to hold on to what she personally knew to be true. After his death in November 1986, when she was twenty, that request grew heavier. 

She had planned to go to law school after Stanford. Grief pulled her instead toward the physical record of the childhood he had kept. 

Decades later the tapes still made absence feel briefly reversible. Hearing his voice again, she could almost imagine him walking back into the room. 

She kept one of his sweaters in her closet. The screen preserved Cary Grant’s face in perfection. The tapes preserved a father laughing with his child, so that she could keep finding him. 🌹
